extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers and journalists interested in media ethics and the Sun's Hillsborough coverage
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how a tabloid newspaper covered a mass-casualty event (the Hillsborough disaster) with emphasis on sourcing, framing, prominence, corrections, and ethical/legal consequences. The page documents specific editorial decisions, examples of failure (false claims, misleading headlines), and the civic responses they produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repeating unreliable claims as fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun drew outrage for its repetition of unreliable claims as fact—including false claims by police officers—that Liverpool supporters were responsible for the incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present unverified allegations (especially from interested parties like police) as factual statements. The article contrasts The Sun's presentation with other papers that either attributed claims or dismissed them. Example anti-pattern: running false allegations on the front page under a definitive headline ('The Truth').

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust sourcing and independent verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun's story relied on sources such as a Conservative MP (Irvine Patnick) and the Whites Press Agency; later accounts say some claims originated with police officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify agency filings and third-party claims independently rather than republishing. The Daily Mirror is cited as having received the same agency filing but dismissed it as untrue—an example of editorial skepticism and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear attribution of claims (avoid asserting source claims as reporter fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other papers reported the police allegations as accusations by the police rather than as established fact (e.g., the Daily Express reported claims as accusations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting contested allegations, attribute them explicitly to their source and avoid framing them as established truth. Proper attribution reduces misleading readers about the strength of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal-risk-aware wording vs ethical transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun used the phrasing 'some fans' for legal reasons, since it could refer to as few as two individuals, demonstrating how legal caution influenced wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal hedging can limit libel risk but may also mask misleading presentation; balance legal risk management with transparent reporting. Note how legal phrasing was used strategically in headlines and copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline framing and prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: The front-page headline 'The Truth' presented allegations as definitive and was a major factor in public outrage; placement and headline size determine perceived authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines and front-page prominence convey authority; sensational, definitive headlines about unverified allegations are high-risk and can cause lasting damage. Editorial decisions on headline wording and placement are a criterion for evaluating coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility, accountability and sincerity of apologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors (notably Kelvin MacKenzie) gave conflicting comments about apologies over years; The Sun issued several apologies (2004, 2012, 2016) with varying reception from victims' families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether apologies are complete, timely, and accompanied by corrective action. Repeated or equivocal apologies (or claims that an apology was coerced) undermine accountability. Example: families called some apologies 'too little, too late' or 'cynical and shameless.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding interference with justice and victim campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Families believe The Sun's coverage interfered in the justice campaign and legal cases that continued until 2016.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting should avoid prejudicing active investigations or legal processes and should consider potential harm to victims' campaigns. Evaluate whether coverage hindered or supported the pursuit of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for public trust and commercial fallout (boycotts, circulation decline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread boycotting in Merseyside followed the coverage; sales in the region reportedly dropped from 55,000 per day to 12,000 per day and the boycott was estimated to have cost owners significant revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess coverage not only on journalistic merits but on measurable social and commercial consequences: loss of readership, sustained boycotts, and reputational damage can indicate serious journalistic failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensationalist or demeaning imagery and language
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include a column that compared Ross Barkley to a gorilla and other demeaning passages by Kelvin MacKenzie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dehumanising language and imagery. Such content can inflame public sentiment, provoke institutional bans, and reflect poor editorial judgement; evaluate whether language respects subjects' dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial skepticism toward official or single-source narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Some newspapers (e.g., Daily Mirror) dismissed the Whites Press Agency filing as untrue, demonstrating skepticism toward a single-source police-influenced narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice requires independent corroboration of official claims and skepticism when a single agency or interested institution supplies explosive allegations. Evaluate whether editors sought corroboration or relied on convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of corrective coverage and proportionality of retractions/apologies
rubrics_metrics.description: After the 2016 inquest The Sun did not carry the verdict on the front page; its apology appeared on pages 8–9 with images of the victims—raising questions about prominence and proportionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider where and how prominently corrections or apologies are published relative to the original offending coverage; prominent, front-page corrections better signal accountability than buried items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional responses: access restrictions and bans as accountability mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Liverpool and Everton denied Sun journalists access to interviews and club facilities; bans were imposed after consultation with victims' families and campaigners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether institutions' restrictions (bans, denial of access) are reasonable responses to journalistic malpractice and how they affect reporting; such reactions are a tangible measure of lost trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term political and social impacts of coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Research cited (American Political Science Review) found the Merseyside boycott led to reduced Euroscepticism compared with comparable areas not boycotting The Sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess media coverage for downstream effects on public opinion and political behaviour; misreporting can have measurable long-term societal consequences beyond immediate reputational harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial decision-making process and newsroom assignment choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Around 20 of The Sun's journalists were sent to Liverpool or Sheffield specifically to 'find negative information' about Liverpool fans and victims, indicating an editorially driven agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether newsroom assignment and commissioning prioritized agenda-driven negative coverage over impartial reporting; commissioning patterns can indicate bias or campaign-style journalism.
